analysis.one_liner: Requires private student lenders to erase loans when the borrower dies or becomes permanently disabled, and shields cosigners.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a 32-25 vote in December 2020, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal student loans already get erased if the borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled. Most private student loans do not, so lenders can keep billing a dead borrower's estate or a parent who cosigned the loan, and a disabled borrower can be hounded for decades. This bill would force private lenders to discharge the loan in those cases, release cosigners when the borrower becomes disabled, and make sure the erased debt is not taxed as income.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers with private student loans who die or become totally and permanently disabled, and the family members and cosigners who would otherwise be stuck with the debt. The bill defines disability using the federal standard and bars lenders from continued monitoring after discharge, so a borrower is not at risk of losing the discharge later. It also blocks lenders from trying to collect after notification, and extends the tax rule that keeps erased loan debt from being counted as income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled borrowers, families, and loan cosigners

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act to require the holder of a private education loan to discharge the student borrower's liability when notified of the borrower's death or total and permanent disability, and bars the lender from attempting to collect afterward [S2] [S4].
When the borrower becomes totally and permanently disabled, the cosigner's obligation is discharged too, and the lender may not monitor the borrower's disability status after discharge [S2] [S4].

The bill also makes the exclusion of discharged student loan debt from gross income permanent, striking the January 1, 2026 sunset in the tax code, so a borrower whose loan is erased does not face a surprise income-tax bill [S2] [S4].
The bill gives the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau authority to write rules implementing the discharge requirement, and gives lenders a one-year lead time before it takes effect [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders and their investors, who lose the ability to collect on loans of borrowers who die or become totally disabled and lose recourse against cosigners in disability cases. The federal Treasury also gives up a small amount of tax revenue because discharged loan debt would never be taxed as income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student lenders and, modestly, the Treasury

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue that mandatory discharges raise their losses on a segment of borrowers, costs that can get priced into interest rates for all private student loan borrowers, though the bill itself contains no offset or lender compensation [S4].
Making the tax exclusion for discharged debt permanent costs the federal government revenue on every future discharge, rather than being limited to a defined window [S2] [S4].
The one-year delayed effective date means borrowers who die or become disabled in the first year after enactment would get no help [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a narrow but badly exposed group: people with private student loans who face death or total disability, plus their cosigners, who currently have no federal protection. The costs fall on lenders and modestly on the Treasury. The bill is straightforwardly targeted, uses the existing federal disability standard, and includes implementation authority for the consumer bureau. The main honest criticism is the unpriced cost shift to lenders and the permanent tax provision, neither of which is large relative to the total private loan market.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 32-25 and it was placed on the calendar in December 2020, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean introduced the bill in September 2019 and it was referred to the Financial Services and Ways and Means Committees [S1] [S6].
In December 2019 the Financial Services Committee met and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 32-25 vote [S6].
The committee formally reported the amended bill on December 21, 2020, the Ways and Means Committee was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar [S6] [S3].
No floor vote ever took place before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders came out ahead: they retained the right to collect on loans of borrowers who die or become totally and permanently disabled, including from cosigners, and no floor vote ever tested the bill.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Held markups in December 2019, amended the bill, and reported it to the House on a 32-25 vote on December 21, 2020.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Casten, Sherman, Pallone, and Kildee).

sides.party_line_note: The committee's 32-25 vote to report the bill tracked the panel's party split, and the sponsor, all four cosponsors, and the committee approval came from Democrats, with no Republican support visible anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill would strip these lenders of their ability to collect on loans of borrowers who die or become totally and permanently disabled, including pursuing cosigners in disability cases. Their interest in continuing those collections runs directly against borrowers and their families, which is exactly what the bill targets [S2] [S4].

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and debt buyers
industries.note: The bill bars collection attempts after notification of death or disability and prohibits post-discharge disability monitoring, shrinking the pool of accounts collectors could pursue [S4].
